1.1 In this Agreement, unless the context otherwise requires:
"Agreement" means this Maintenance Agreement MA-2023-018 together with all Schedules and Annexures hereto;
"Business Day" means any day (other than a Saturday, Sunday, or public holiday in the Federal Republic of Nigeria) on which banks in Lagos and Kaduna are open for general banking business;
"Change Order" means a written instruction issued by the Client pursuant to Clause 8;
"Client's Representative" means the person nominated by the Client in writing as its authorised representative for the purposes of this Agreement;
"Confidential Information" has the meaning ascribed to it in Clause 12;
"Defect" means any fault, failure, malfunction, or deviation from the performance specifications set out in Schedule 2;
"Effective Date" means 2023-04-01;
"Force Majeure" has the meaning ascribed to it in Clause 15;
"Maintenance Services" means the services described in Schedule 1;
"Month" means a calendar month;
"Service Year" means each successive period of twelve (12) consecutive Months commencing on the Effective Date or on any anniversary thereof;
"Service Provider's Representative" means the person nominated by the Service Provider in writing as its authorised representative for the purposes of this Agreement;
"Site" means the Client's main manufacturing facility along Zaria Road, Kaduna, Kaduna State, Nigeria.

1.2 Clause headings are for convenience only and shall not affect the interpretation of this Agreement.

1.3 Words importing the singular shall include the plural and vice versa, and words importing any gender shall include all genders.

2. SCOPE OF MAINTENANCE SERVICES

2.1 The Service Provider shall provide the Maintenance Services at the Site during the term of this Agreement, in accordance with the service description set out in Schedule 1 and the performance standards set out in Schedule 2.

2.2 The Maintenance Services shall include, without limitation:
(a) scheduled preventive maintenance visits to the Installation at the frequency specified in Schedule 1;
(b) corrective maintenance and repair of Defects reported by the Client or identified by the Service Provider during scheduled visits;
(c) 24-hour remote monitoring of the Installation's performance data, with a written monthly performance report to be delivered to the Client's Representative by the fifth (5th) Business Day of the following Month;
(d) replacement of consumable parts and components, the cost of which shall be borne by the Service Provider up to the annual limit specified in Schedule 3; and
(e) emergency call-out response within the response times specified in Schedule 2.

The Maintenance Agreement MA-2023-018 states that the contract_start_date is 2023-04-01. Record status: current.

2.3 The Maintenance Services do not include:
(a) major capital replacement of solar panels, inverters, or transformers, except where such replacement is required due to a Defect caused by the Service Provider's negligence or breach of this Agreement;
(b) works required due to vandalism, theft, lightning strikes, flooding, or other events of Force Majeure; or
(c) any modification, upgrade, or extension of the Installation not forming part of the original specification.

3. TERM AND COMMENCEMENT

3.1 This Agreement shall commence on the Effective Date and shall continue in force for a period of five (5) Service Years, unless terminated earlier in accordance with the provisions of Clause 14.

3.2 Either Party may, by giving not less than ninety (90) days' written notice to the other Party, propose amendments to the scope or pricing of the Maintenance Services at the commencement of each Service Year; provided that any such amendment shall take effect only upon execution of a written Change Order in accordance with Clause 8.

4. FEES AND PAYMENT

4.1 The Client shall pay the Service Provider the annual maintenance fee (the "Annual Fee") set out in Schedule 3, payable in four (4) equal quarterly instalments in advance.
(d) Remote Monitoring: The Service Provider shall monitor the Installation's performance data on a 24-hour basis and shall alert the Client's Representative within two (2) hours of detecting any anomaly that may indicate a Defect or a reduction in performance below the levels specified in Schedule 2.

5.2 If the Service Provider fails to meet any of the service levels set out in Clause 5.1, the Client shall be entitled to a service credit calculated in accordance with Schedule 2, provided that:

(a) the Client has given the Service Provider written notice of the failure within fourteen (14) days of the date on which the failure occurred or ought reasonably to have been detected; and

(b) the failure was not caused by the Client, an event of Force Majeure, or any other circumstances beyond the Service Provider's reasonable control.

5.4 The Parties acknowledge that the service levels set out in this Clause 5 are a fundamental term of this Agreement, and that the Client would not have entered into this Agreement without the Service Provider's commitment to meet such service levels.

6. REPORTING AND RECORD-KEEPING

6.1 The Service Provider shall deliver to the Client's Representative the following reports:

(a) a monthly performance report, as described in Clause 2.2(c), which shall include, at minimum, the following information:

(i) the aggregate energy output of the Installation for the preceding Month;

(ii) the availability of the Installation, expressed as a percentage of the total possible operating hours;

(iii) a summary of all alarms, faults, and anomalies detected during the preceding Month, together with the action taken in respect of each;

(iv) the results of all scheduled maintenance activities completed during the preceding Month; and

(v) a forecast of any planned maintenance activities for the following Month.

The Maintenance Agreement MA-2023-018 specifies a contract_term_years of 5. Record status: current.

(b) an annual maintenance report, to be delivered within thirty (30) days of the anniversary of the Effective Date, which shall include a detailed analysis of the Installation's performance over the preceding Service Year, a summary of all maintenance activities undertaken, and recommendations for any capital improvements or upgrades that the Service Provider considers advisable.

(c) a written incident report for each Emergency Defect, to be delivered within five (5) Business Days of the resolution of the incident, which shall include a root cause analysis, the corrective actions taken, and recommendations to prevent recurrence.

6.2 All reports shall be delivered in electronic format to the email address specified in the Client's Details, unless the Client's Representative requests a hard copy.

6.4 The Service Provider shall maintain a log of all maintenance activities, including scheduled visits, corrective repairs, and emergency call-outs. The log shall record the date and time of each activity, the personnel involved, the work performed, and the parts or consumables used. The log shall be made available to the Client's Representative upon request.

7. CLIENT'S OBLIGATIONS

7.1 The Client shall:

(a) provide the Service Provider with safe and unhindered access to the Installation during normal working hours and, in the case of an Emergency Defect, at any time, upon reasonable notice;

(b) provide a suitable and safe working environment for the Service Provider's personnel, including access to water, electricity, and sanitation facilities;

(c) ensure that the Installation is not subject to any unauthorised modification, interference, or operation outside the parameters specified in the manufacturer's documentation, except with the prior written consent of the Service Provider;

(d) promptly notify the Service Provider of any known or suspected Defect, or any event that may give rise to a claim under this Agreement;

(e) provide the Service Provider with all necessary information and documentation relating to the Installation, including as-built drawings, equipment manuals, and warranty certificates; and

(f) obtain and maintain all necessary permits, licences, and consents required for the operation of the Installation.
8. LIABILITY AND INDEMNITY

8.1 Subject to Clause 8.2, each Party shall be liable to the other Party for any direct loss, damage, or expense arising out of or in connection with this Agreement, whether in contract, tort (including negligence), breach of statutory duty, or otherwise, to the extent that such loss, damage, or expense is caused by that Party's breach of this Agreement or by that Party's negligence.

8.2 Neither Party shall be liable to the other Party for any indirect or consequential loss or damage, including but not limited to loss of profits, loss of revenue, loss of business, loss of goodwill, loss of anticipated savings, or loss of data, whether arising in contract, tort (including negligence), or otherwise.

8.3 The Service Provider's aggregate liability under or in connection with this Agreement, whether in contract, tort (including negligence), breach of statutory duty, or otherwise, shall not exceed the total Service Fees paid or payable by the Client to the Service Provider during the twelve (12) months immediately preceding the date on which the cause of action arose.

8.4 Nothing in this Agreement shall operate to exclude or limit either Party's liability for:
(a) death or personal injury caused by negligence;
(b) fraud or fraudulent misrepresentation;
(c) any matter for which it would be unlawful for the Parties to exclude or attempt to exclude liability.

8.5 The Client shall indemnify and hold harmless the Service Provider, its officers, employees, and agents from and against any and all claims, demands, losses, damages, costs, and expenses (including reasonable legal fees) arising out of or in connection with:
(a) any breach by the Client of its obligations under this Agreement;
(b) any negligent act or omission of the Client, its officers, employees, or agents;
(c) any claim by a third party arising from the Client's use or operation of the Installation, except to the extent that such claim arises from the Service Provider's negligence or breach of this Agreement.

8.6 The Service Provider shall indemnify and hold harmless the Client from and against any claims, demands, losses, damages, costs, and expenses (including reasonable legal fees) arising out of or in connection with:
(a) any breach by the Service Provider of its obligations under this Agreement;
(b) any negligent act or omission of the Service Provider, its officers, employees, or agents in the performance of the Services.

8.7 The provisions of this Clause 8 shall survive the expiration or termination of this Agreement.

9. INSURANCE

9.1 The Service Provider shall, at its own cost, obtain and maintain for the duration of this Agreement the following insurance policies with reputable insurers:
(a) public liability insurance with a minimum limit of indemnity of Five Hundred Million Naira (N500,000,000.00) per occurrence;
(b) employer's liability insurance with a minimum limit of indemnity of Fifty Million Naira (N50,000,000.00) per occurrence;
(c) professional indemnity insurance with a minimum limit of indemnity of Two Hundred Million Naira (N200,000,000.00) per claim;
(d) comprehensive motor vehicle insurance in respect of all vehicles used in connection with the provision of the Services.

9.2 The Service Provider shall, upon request, provide the Client with certificates of insurance evidencing the cover required under Clause 9.1. The Service Provider shall notify the Client promptly in writing of any material change to, or cancellation of, any such insurance policy.

10. CONFIDENTIALITY

10.1 Each Party (the "Receiving Party") shall keep confidential and shall not use or disclose to any person, without the prior written consent of the other Party (the "Disclosing Party"), any Confidential Information of the Disclosing Party obtained in connection with this Agreement.

10.2 For the purposes of this Agreement, "Confidential Information" means all information disclosed by one Party to the other, whether before or after the date of this Agreement, in any form or medium, that is marked as confidential or that ought reasonably to be understood to be confidential, including but not limited to:
(a) the terms of this Agreement;
(b) technical data, specifications, drawings, and designs relating to the Installation;
(c) business plans, financial information, and customer data;
(d) any information relating to the Service Provider's pricing, methodologies, or proprietary tools.

Change Request Number: CR-2024-007
Project / Asset: Egbin Solar Farm — Phase 2 (22 MWp)
Originating Section: O&M — Solar Plant Operations
Request Title: Replacement of DC String Combiner Box Fuses with Rated Surge-Protected Units

Date of Submission: 2024-06-10
Submitted By: Engr. T. Adeyemi (O&M Supervisor)
Priority: Medium

Description of Change:
The existing DC string combiner boxes at the Egbin Solar Farm are fitted with standard gPV fuses rated at 1000 V DC. Following the lightning event of 2024-05-28, three combiner boxes (CB-04, CB-11, CB-17) experienced fuse blown indications despite no confirmed string fault. Inspection revealed that the fuses had operated due to induced surge currents rather than actual overcurrent conditions. The proposed change is to replace the standard fuses with surge-protected fuse units (rated 1000 V DC, 15 A) that incorporate integral transient suppression, in all 28 combiner boxes across the plant.

Justification:
The current fuse specification does not provide adequate protection against transient surge events, which are common during the rainy season in Ogun State. The proposed units will reduce nuisance tripping, minimise downtime, and protect downstream inverter inputs. The change aligns with the manufacturer's recommendation following the incident review.

Impact Assessment (prepared by Engineering Services, 2024-06-12):
- Safety: No negative impact. New fuses have similar breaking capacity and arc-quenching properties.
- Performance: Expected reduction in unplanned outages related to fuse operations.
- Cost: Estimated ₦4.8 million including labour and disposal of replaced units.
- Schedule: Replacement to be carried out during scheduled maintenance window — Q3 2024.
- Spares: Existing stock of standard fuses (48 units) will be returned to central stores for use on other sites.

Approval Decision:
The Change Request CR-2024-007 has a status of approved. Record status: current. This decision was taken by the CCB at its sitting of 2024-06-15 and is effective immediately.

Change Request Number: CR-2024-008
Project / Asset: Apo Wind Farm — Turbine Foundation Inspection Programme
Originating Section: Civil & Structural Engineering
Request Title: Amendment to Foundation Inspection Frequency for T-12, T-14, T-23

Date of Submission: 2024-06-12
Submitted By: Engr. K. Bello (Civil Engineer II)
Priority: High

Description of Change:
The current inspection regime for wind turbine foundations at the Apo Wind Farm requires a detailed visual inspection every 12 months and an ultrasonic thickness survey every 24 months. The proposed change is to increase the frequency of detailed visual inspections for Turbines T-12, T-14, and T-23 to every 6 months, and to bring forward the ultrasonic survey for these three foundations to Q4 2024, rather than their scheduled dates in 2025.

Justification:
Cracks were observed in the grout interface of T-12 during the routine inspection of 2024-05-20. Similar micro-cracking was subsequently identified on T-14 and T-23 during a targeted follow-up. While the cracks are currently assessed as non-structural (width < 0.3 mm), the geotechnical report for the site indicates variable soil settlement zones beneath these specific turbines. The increased frequency is intended to provide early warning of any progression.

3.3 CR-2024-011 — Use of Alternative Lubricant for Gearbox Maintenance, Apo Wind Farm
Originating Section: Mechanical Maintenance
Submitted By: Engr. F. Osei (Mechanical Engineer I)
Date of Submission: 2024-06-14
Priority: Medium

The Board considered a request to approve the use of an alternative gearbox lubricant (ISO VG 320 synthetic) for the wind turbine gearboxes at Apo Wind Farm. The request was prompted by recurring supply delays for the OEM-specified lubricant, which has caused two maintenance windows to be postponed in the last six months.
Originating Section: Electrical Maintenance
Submitted By: Engr. N. Bello (Maintenance Superintendent)
Date of Submission: 2024-06-14
Priority: High

The Board considered a request to extend the existing maintenance contract for the 33/11 kV substation transformers at the Jos cluster by twelve months. The current contract, held by TransServe Nigeria Limited, is due to expire on 2024-09-30. The extension is sought to allow sufficient time for a competitive tendering process for a new contract, which was originally scheduled to commence in July 2024 but has been delayed due to the late receipt of the asset condition reports from the Jos regional office.

The Board reviewed the performance of TransServe over the current contract period. The contractor has achieved a mean time to repair of 4.2 days against a contractual target of 5 days, and has completed all scheduled preventive maintenance visits for the 2023-2024 period. However, the Board noted two instances of delayed response to emergency call-outs, both of which were attributed to the contractor's mobilisation from their Kaduna base. The contractor has since established a small satellite workshop in Jos, which is expected to improve response times.

The extension is proposed on the same terms and conditions as the current contract, with no change to the contract sum of ₦62 million per annum. The Board noted that the delay in the tendering process was partly attributable to the late submission of asset condition reports, and directed the Jos regional office to ensure that such reports are submitted at least sixty days before the expiry of any future contract.

Decision: Approved for a twelve-month extension, effective from 2024-10-01, on the same terms and conditions. The tendering process for the new contract shall be completed no later than 2025-06-30.

3.5 CR-2024-013 — Installation of Bird Deterrents at Kainji Transmission Line Sections

Originating Section: Transmission Lines
Submitted By: Mr. T. Eze (Lines Supervisor)
Date of Submission: 2024-06-14
Priority: Low

The Change Request CR-2024-007 scope_description is 'Add condition monitoring sensors to inverter bays'. Record status: current.

The Board considered a request to install bird deterrent devices on selected transmission line sections near Kainji Lake. The request was prompted by a series of transient faults on the 132 kV line between Kainji and Bida, which have been attributed to bird streamers and nesting activity on the cross-arms. The faults have caused intermittent tripping, with a total of seven trips recorded between January and May 2024, each lasting between 40 milliseconds and 2 seconds.

The proposal covers the installation of 320 bird flight diverters on the most affected spans, at an estimated cost of ₦8.2 million, including materials, labour, and a two-year warranty. The diverters are of the spiral type, which are reported to be effective for the species present in the area, including the African fish eagle and the grey heron.

The Board noted that the fault data had not been fully analysed to confirm that the bird activity was the sole cause of the trips. A review of the disturbance records showed that two of the seven trips occurred during periods of lightning activity, and one occurred during a period of high wind. The remaining four trips, however, could not be attributed to any other cause and coincided with observations of bird activity reported by the local community.

Decision: Approved in principle, subject to a detailed fault analysis to confirm the bird-related trips. The analysis shall be completed by the Protection and Control Section and submitted to the Board within four weeks. If the analysis confirms the bird-related cause, the installation shall proceed as proposed.

3.8 CR-2025-002 — Modification of Access Road Maintenance Contract for the Zamfara Solar Farm

The Board considered a proposal to modify the existing access road maintenance contract for the Zamfara solar farm. The current contract, which was awarded in March 2024, covers routine grading and pothole patching of the 23-kilometre access road from the main highway to the plant gate. The proposal seeks to expand the scope of works to include the reinforcement of three culvert crossings that were damaged during the December 2024 rains, and the installation of drainage channels along two sections of the road that are prone to flooding.

The originating section reported that the December rains had caused significant erosion at the culvert crossings, with one culvert (at kilometre 14) now partially collapsed. The road has been passable only with difficulty since the rains, and the section has received complaints from plant operators regarding delays in the delivery of spare parts and consumables. Bakare observed that the proposed modification was within the ±10% variation limit stipulated in the contract conditions, and that the additional cost could be accommodated within the existing contingency allocation for the plant. He recommended that the change order be processed expeditiously, given the operational impact of the road condition.

Mr. A. I. Musa confirmed that the draft change order was in order, but noted that the contractor's insurance cover would need to be extended to cover the additional works. 3.9 CR-2024-015 — Revision of Spare Parts Stock Holding Levels for the Katsina Wind Farm

Originating Section: Materials Management
Submitted By: Mrs. F. O. Adebayo (Materials Manager)
Date of Submission: 2024-11-20
Priority: Low

The Board considered a proposal to revise the minimum and maximum stock holding levels for spare parts held at the Katsina wind farm. The current levels were established at the time of commissioning and have not been reviewed since. The proposal is based on an analysis of consumption data over the past eighteen months, which shows that the holding levels for certain high-value components are excessive, while those for several consumable items are inadequate.

The proposal covers a total of 47 stock items. For 12 items, the maximum holding level is to be reduced, releasing an estimated ₦4.1 million in working capital. For 29 items, the minimum holding level is to be increased to prevent stockouts, which have occurred on three occasions during the review period.
Proposed Change
The originating section proposes that the scope of the preventive maintenance contract be extended to include the following:

i. Quarterly oil sampling of all 120 tracker gearboxes.
ii. Laboratory analysis of samples for viscosity, water content, particle count, and ferrous debris.
iii. Provision of a written report within ten working days of sample collection.
iv. A recommendation on whether any gearbox requires further inspection or oil replacement based on the analysis results.

The proposed change does not include the cost of replacement oil, which would be charged separately under the existing maintenance contract.

Cost Estimate
The estimated annual cost of the proposed change is ₦14.5 million. This estimate was prepared by the originating section based on quotations obtained from three accredited laboratories. The estimate includes the cost of sample collection, laboratory analysis, reporting, and the provision of sample bottles and labels. It does not include the cost of replacement oil or any additional labour required to replace oil where analysis indicates contamination.

Justification
The originating section states that the proposed change is justified by the following considerations:

i. The reduction in unplanned downtime and associated loss of generation.
ii. The avoidance of damage to tracker components, which are not covered by the manufacturer's warranty beyond the initial twelve-month period.
iii. The availability of data on oil condition, which would assist in optimising the lubrication schedule and extending gearbox life.

The Change Request CR-2025-002 submission_date is 2025-01-10. Record status: current.

The originating section estimates that the proposed change would pay for itself if it prevents two gearbox failures over a twelve-month period.

Discussion
Engr. S. A. Yusuf asked whether the oil analysis could be undertaken by the plant's own maintenance staff rather than by an external laboratory. The originating section explained that the plant does not currently have the necessary laboratory equipment or trained personnel, and that the cost of acquiring the equipment and training staff would exceed the cost of the proposed external service for the initial two-year period.

Mrs. C. N. Okafor requested clarification on the basis of the cost estimate, noting that the annual cost of ₦14.5 million appeared to be significantly higher than the cost of the existing preventive maintenance contract. The originating section explained that the existing contract was entered into before the commissioning of the plant and was based on the manufacturer's standard maintenance schedule. The cost of oil analysis reflects the number of gearboxes and the frequency of sampling, and is comparable to the cost of similar programmes at other solar plants in the region.

Mr. A. I. Musa asked whether the proposed change would require an extension of the contractor's insurance cover, as had been the case for the drainage channel works considered earlier in the meeting. The originating section confirmed that the existing insurance cover under the maintenance contract would not extend to the additional works, and that the contractor would be required to provide evidence of extended insurance cover before the commencement of the additional works. Mr. Musa directed that this requirement be included in the change order.

Ms. F. O. Eze noted that the Change Request CR-2025-002 submission_date is 2025-01-10, and asked whether the delay in considering the request had had any operational impact. The originating section reported that a further gearbox failure had occurred on 2025-01-28, and that the plant had been operating with one tracker out of service since that date. The failure had been reported to the contractor, but the contractor had advised that the repair would be covered under the existing contract as a breakdown call-out. The originating section stated that the failure reinforced the urgency of the proposed change.
Engr. S. O. Adeyemi presented an updated operational impact assessment. He stated that the plant had experienced a further gearbox failure on 2025-01-28, and that one tracker had been out of service since that date. The breakdown had been reported to the contractor, who had advised that the repair would be covered under the existing contract as a breakdown call-out. Engr. Adeyemi noted that the repeated failures had led to a cumulative loss of generation estimated at 1,840 MWh between October 2024 and January 2025, and that the current outage was expected to persist until the next scheduled maintenance window unless the contractor could be mobilised earlier. He reiterated that the current maintenance window of 24 hours was insufficient to carry out the necessary inspections and repairs on all 120 trackers, and that the failure of a single gearbox could take up to 12 hours to rectify, leaving no time for the preventive checks that were intended to reduce the frequency of such failures.

The Chair asked whether the contractor had provided any indication of the cause of the January failure. Engr. Adeyemi replied that the contractor had not yet submitted a formal failure report, but that the preliminary indication was that the failure was consistent with the earlier incidents, namely a breakdown of the gearbox bearing due to inadequate lubrication. He added that the contractor had, however, noted in an informal communication that the plant’s lubrication schedule might not be aligned with the manufacturer’s recommendations, and that the contractor would provide a detailed report after the next maintenance visit.

Ms. F. O. Eze asked whether the Board had considered the option of carrying out the repairs under the existing contract as breakdown call-outs, rather than extending the maintenance window. Engr. Adeyemi explained that breakdown call-outs were subject to a response time of 72 hours and were charged at a premium rate of ₦2.5 million per call-out. He noted that the plant had already incurred three call-out charges in the past four months, and that the cost of a planned maintenance window extension would be lower than the cumulative cost of further call-outs. He also noted that the breakdown call-outs did not include the preventive checks that were essential to reducing the frequency of failures.

Mr. A. I. Musa asked whether the proposed change would require any amendment to the contractor’s scope of works under the existing contract. Engr. Adeyemi confirmed that the scope of works would remain unchanged, and that the proposed change only affected the duration of the maintenance window. Mr. Musa noted that this would simplify the legal drafting of the change order, and that the main legal consideration would be the effect on the contract completion date and the insurance cover.

**1.2 Cost Impact Assessment**

Mrs. J. O. Umeh presented the updated cost impact assessment. She noted that the cost of extending the maintenance window from 24 hours to 48 hours would be ₦8.2 million per maintenance visit, which was based on the contractor’s rate of ₦342,000 per hour for the additional 24 hours. She noted that this figure excluded the cost of consumables and spare parts, which would be charged at cost. She also noted that the cost of the extended window would be offset by the avoided cost of breakdown call-outs, which were estimated at ₦2.5 million per incident. Based on the failure rate observed in the past six months, the Board could expect to avoid between two and three call-outs per quarter, resulting in a net saving of between ₦1.8 million and ₦4.3 million per quarter.

Mrs. Umeh also noted that the cost of the extended window would be partially offset by the reduction in lost generation. She estimated that the extended window would allow the maintenance team to complete all preventive checks and repairs in a single visit, reducing the likelihood of a breakdown occurring shortly after the maintenance visit. She noted that the plant had experienced a failure within two weeks of the last two maintenance visits, and that the extended window would allow the team to carry out a more thorough inspection of the gearboxes, including a visual inspection of the oil seals and a check of the torque settings on the mounting bolts.

**1.3 Operational Readiness and Scheduling Impact**

Engr. T. A. Bakare (Maintenance Manager) submitted a memorandum dated 2025-01-09 regarding the operational readiness for the proposed 48-hour maintenance window. He confirmed that the site maintenance crew currently operates two shifts of ten hours each, with a four-hour overlap for handover and safety briefings. Under the existing 24-hour window, this shift pattern allows for only 20 hours of effective working time, with the remaining four hours consumed by mobilisation, isolation, and re-commissioning.

Engr. Bakare noted that the extension to 48 hours would permit the crew to complete the full preventive maintenance schedule for the wind turbine gearboxes, including the inspection of high-speed and intermediate shaft bearings, without the need to defer any checks to a subsequent visit. He further noted that the extended window would also allow for the replacement of the oil filters on all three units, which was previously deferred due to time constraints. The memorandum is attached as Annex 3 to this file.

The CCB noted that the extension of the maintenance window would not affect the frequency of scheduled maintenance visits, which remains at one visit per quarter per turbine. The change would, however, require the contractor to provide an additional standby generator for the duration of the extended window, as the site’s main supply is not available during the maintenance period. Engr. Bakare confirmed that this would not constitute a change to the scope of works, but would be treated as a site facility arrangement.

**1.4 Insurance and Warranty Considerations**

Mrs. J. O. Umeh presented a legal note on the insurance implications of the extended maintenance window. She noted that the current all-risk policy covers the plant during maintenance, but the policy defines a maintenance window as a period not exceeding 24 hours. An extension to 48 hours would therefore require the insurer to be notified and the policy to be endorsed. Mrs. Umeh confirmed that the insurer had been approached informally, and that the endorsement would be issued at no additional premium, provided the extension was approved by the CCB before the end of the current policy year.

Mrs. Umeh also noted that the extended window would not affect the warranty on the gearboxes, as the warranty terms refer to the completion of the manufacturer’s recommended maintenance schedule, and not to the duration of any single maintenance visit. Mr. Adewale recommended that the crew be split into three shifts of eight hours each, with a mandatory rest period of 30 minutes between shifts. He also recommended that an additional first-aid kit be stationed at the base of each turbine.

The CCB noted that the contractor’s proposed shift pattern for the extended window was based on two shifts of 12 hours each, which would not comply with the site HSE policy. Change Request Number: CR-2024-007
Project / Asset: Egbin Solar Farm — Phase 2 (22 MWp)
Originating Section: O&M — Solar Plant Operations
Request Title: Replacement of DC String Combiner Box Fuses with Rated Surge-Protected Units

Date of Submission: 2024-06-10
Submitted By: Engr. T. Adeyemi (O&M Supervisor)
Priority: Medium

Description of Change:
The existing DC string combiner boxes at the Egbin Solar Farm are fitted with standard gPV fuses rated at 1000 V DC. Following the lightning event of 2024-05-28, three combiner boxes (CB-04, CB-11, CB-17) experienced fuse blown indications despite no confirmed string fault. Inspection revealed that the fuses had operated due to induced surge currents rather than actual overcurrent conditions. The proposed change is to replace the standard fuses with surge-protected fuse units (rated 1000 V DC, 15 A) that incorporate integral transient suppression, in all 28 combiner boxes across the plant.

Justification:
The current fuse specification does not provide adequate protection against transient surge events, which are common during the rainy season in Ogun State. The proposed units will reduce nuisance tripping, minimise downtime, and protect downstream inverter inputs. The change aligns with the manufacturer's recommendation following the incident review.

Impact Assessment (prepared by Engineering Services, 2024-06-12):
- Safety: No negative impact. New fuses have similar breaking capacity and arc-quenching properties.
- Performance: Expected reduction in unplanned outages related to fuse operations.
- Cost: Estimated ₦4.8 million including labour and disposal of replaced units.
- Schedule: Replacement to be carried out during scheduled maintenance window — Q3 2024.
- Spares: Existing stock of standard fuses (48 units) will be returned to central stores for use on other sites.

Approval Decision:
The Change Request CR-2024-007 has a status of approved. Record status: current. This decision was taken by the CCB at its sitting of 2024-06-15 and is effective immediately.

Change Request Number: CR-2024-008
Project / Asset: Apo Wind Farm — Turbine Foundation Inspection Programme
Originating Section: Civil & Structural Engineering
Request Title: Amendment to Foundation Inspection Frequency for T-12, T-14, T-23

Date of Submission: 2024-06-12
Submitted By: Engr. K. Bello (Civil Engineer II)
Priority: High

Description of Change:
The current inspection regime for wind turbine foundations at the Apo Wind Farm requires a detailed visual inspection every 12 months and an ultrasonic thickness survey every 24 months. The proposed change is to increase the frequency of detailed visual inspections for Turbines T-12, T-14, and T-23 to every 6 months, and to bring forward the ultrasonic survey for these three foundations to Q4 2024, rather than their scheduled dates in 2025.

Justification:
Cracks were observed in the grout interface of T-12 during the routine inspection of 2024-05-20. Similar micro-cracking was subsequently identified on T-14 and T-23 during a targeted follow-up. While the cracks are currently assessed as non-structural (width < 0.3 mm), the geotechnical report for the site indicates variable soil settlement zones beneath these specific turbines. The increased frequency is intended to provide early warning of any progression.

The contractor has achieved a mean time to repair of 4.2 days against a contractual target of 5 days, and has completed all scheduled preventive maintenance visits for the 2023-2024 period. The contractor has since established a small satellite workshop in Jos, which is expected to improve response times.

The extension is proposed on the same terms and conditions as the current contract, with no change to the contract sum of ₦62 million per annum. The Board noted that the delay in the tendering process was partly attributable to the late submission of asset condition reports, and directed the Jos regional office to ensure that such reports are submitted at least sixty days before the expiry of any future contract.

The Board considered a request to install bird deterrent devices on selected transmission line sections near Kainji Lake. The request was prompted by a series of transient faults on the 132 kV line between Kainji and Bida, which have been attributed to bird streamers and nesting activity on the cross-arms. The faults have caused intermittent tripping, with a total of seven trips recorded between January and May 2024, each lasting between 40 milliseconds and 2 seconds.

The proposal covers the installation of 320 bird flight diverters on the most affected spans, at an estimated cost of ₦8.2 million, including materials, labour, and a two-year warranty. The diverters are of the spiral type, which are reported to be effective for the species present in the area, including the African fish eagle and the grey heron.

The Board noted that the fault data had not been fully analysed to confirm that the bird activity was the sole cause of the trips. A review of the disturbance records showed that two of the seven trips occurred during periods of lightning activity, and one occurred during a period of high wind. The remaining four trips, however, could not be attributed to any other cause and coincided with observations of bird activity reported by the local community.

Decision: Approved in principle, subject to a detailed fault analysis to confirm the bird-related trips. The analysis shall be completed by the Protection and Control Section and submitted to the Board within four weeks. If the analysis confirms the bird-related cause, the installation shall proceed as proposed.

The proposal seeks to expand the scope of works to include the reinforcement of three culvert crossings that were damaged during the December 2024 rains, and the installation of drainage channels along two sections of the road that are prone to flooding.

The originating section reported that the December rains had caused significant erosion at the culvert crossings, with one culvert (at kilometre 14) now partially collapsed. The road has been passable only with difficulty since the rains, and the section has received complaints from plant operators regarding delays in the delivery of spare parts and consumables. The estimated cost of the additional works is ₦3.6 million, which includes materials, labour, and a six-month defect liability period.

The Board noted that the existing contract does not contain a provision for variations of this nature, and that the modification would therefore require a formal change order. The proposal included a draft change order, which was reviewed by the Legal and Compliance section during the meeting.

Submitted By: Mrs. F. O. Adebayo (Materials Manager)
Date of Submission: 2024-11-20
Priority: Low

The Board considered a proposal to revise the minimum and maximum stock holding levels for spare parts held at the Katsina wind farm. The current levels were established at the time of commissioning and have not been reviewed since. The proposal is based on an analysis of consumption data over the past eighteen months, which shows that the holding levels for certain high-value components are excessive, while those for several consumable items are inadequate.

The proposal covers a total of 47 stock items. For 12 items, the maximum holding level is to be reduced, releasing an estimated ₦4.1 million in working capital. For 29 items, the minimum holding level is to be increased to prevent stockouts, which have occurred on three occasions during the review period.

Proposed Change
The originating section proposes that the scope of the preventive maintenance contract be extended to include the following:

i. Quarterly oil sampling of all 120 tracker gearboxes.
ii. Laboratory analysis of samples for viscosity, water content, particle count, and ferrous debris.
iii. Provision of a written report within ten working days of sample collection.
iv. A recommendation on whether any gearbox requires further inspection or oil replacement based on the analysis results.

The proposed change does not include the cost of replacement oil, which would be charged separately under the existing maintenance contract.

Cost Estimate
The estimated annual cost of the proposed change is ₦14.5 million. This estimate was prepared by the originating section based on quotations obtained from three accredited laboratories. The estimate includes the cost of sample collection, laboratory analysis, reporting, and the provision of sample bottles and labels. It does not include the cost of replacement oil or any additional labour required to replace oil where analysis indicates contamination.

Justification
The originating section states that the proposed change is justified by the following considerations:

i. The reduction in unplanned downtime and associated loss of generation.
ii. The avoidance of damage to tracker components, which are not covered by the manufacturer's warranty beyond the initial twelve-month period.
iii. The availability of data on oil condition, which would assist in optimising the lubrication schedule and extending gearbox life.

The Change Request CR-2025-002 submission_date is 2025-01-10. Record status: current.

The originating section estimates that the proposed change would pay for itself if it prevents two gearbox failures over a twelve-month period.

Discussion
Engr. S. A. Yusuf asked whether the oil analysis could be undertaken by the plant's own maintenance staff rather than by an external laboratory. The originating section explained that the plant does not currently have the necessary laboratory equipment or trained personnel, and that the cost of acquiring the equipment and training staff would exceed the cost of the proposed external service for the initial two-year period.

Mrs. C. N. Okafor requested clarification on the basis of the cost estimate, noting that the annual cost of ₦14.5 million appeared to be significantly higher than the cost of the existing preventive maintenance contract. The originating section explained that the existing contract was entered into before the commissioning of the plant and was based on the manufacturer's standard maintenance schedule. The cost of oil analysis reflects the number of gearboxes and the frequency of sampling, and is comparable to the cost of similar programmes at other solar plants in the region.

Mr. A. I. Musa asked whether the proposed change would require an extension of the contractor's insurance cover, as had been the case for the drainage channel works considered earlier in the meeting. The originating section confirmed that the existing insurance cover under the maintenance contract would not extend to the additional works, and that the contractor would be required to provide evidence of extended insurance cover before the commencement of the additional works. Mr. Musa directed that this requirement be included in the change order.

Ms. F. O. Eze noted that the Change Request CR-2025-002 submission_date is 2025-01-10, and asked whether the delay in considering the request had had any operational impact. The originating section reported that a further gearbox failure had occurred on 2025-01-28, and that the plant had been operating with one tracker out of service since that date. The failure had been reported to the contractor, but the contractor had advised that the repair would be covered under the existing contract as a breakdown call-out. The originating section stated that the failure reinforced the urgency of the proposed change.

Engr. S. O. Adeyemi presented an updated operational impact assessment. He stated that the plant had experienced a further gearbox failure on 2025-01-28, and that one tracker had been out of service since that date. The breakdown had been reported to the contractor, who had advised that the repair would be covered under the existing contract as a breakdown call-out. Engr. Adeyemi noted that the repeated failures had led to a cumulative loss of generation estimated at 1,840 MWh between October 2024 and January 2025, and that the current outage was expected to persist until the next scheduled maintenance window unless the contractor could be mobilised earlier. He reiterated that the current maintenance window of 24 hours was insufficient to carry out the necessary inspections and repairs on all 120 trackers, and that the failure of a single gearbox could take up to 12 hours to rectify, leaving no time for the preventive checks that were intended to reduce the frequency of such failures.

The Chair asked whether the contractor had provided any indication of the cause of the January failure. Engr. Adeyemi replied that the contractor had not yet submitted a formal failure report, but that the preliminary indication was that the failure was consistent with the earlier incidents, namely a breakdown of the gearbox bearing due to inadequate lubrication. He added that the contractor had, however, noted in an informal communication that the plant’s lubrication schedule might not be aligned with the manufacturer’s recommendations, and that the contractor would provide a detailed report after the next maintenance visit.

Ms. F. O. Eze asked whether the Board had considered the option of carrying out the repairs under the existing contract as breakdown call-outs, rather than extending the maintenance window. Engr. Adeyemi explained that breakdown call-outs were subject to a response time of 72 hours and were charged at a premium rate of ₦2.5 million per call-out. He noted that the plant had already incurred three call-out charges in the past four months, and that the cost of a planned maintenance window extension would be lower than the cumulative cost of further call-outs. He also noted that the breakdown call-outs did not include the preventive checks that were essential to reducing the frequency of failures.

Mr. A. I. Musa asked whether the proposed change would require any amendment to the contractor’s scope of works under the existing contract. Engr. Adeyemi confirmed that the scope of works would remain unchanged, and that the proposed change only affected the duration of the maintenance window. Mr. Musa noted that this would simplify the legal drafting of the change order, and that the main legal consideration would be the effect on the contract completion date and the insurance cover.

**1.2 Cost Impact Assessment**

Mrs. J. O. Umeh presented the updated cost impact assessment. She noted that the cost of extending the maintenance window from 24 hours to 48 hours would be ₦8.2 million per maintenance visit, which was based on the contractor’s rate of ₦342,000 per hour for the additional 24 hours. She noted that this figure excluded the cost of consumables and spare parts, which would be charged at cost. She also noted that the cost of the extended window would be offset by the avoided cost of breakdown call-outs, which were estimated at ₦2.5 million per incident. Based on the failure rate observed in the past six months, the Board could expect to avoid between two and three call-outs per quarter, resulting in a net saving of between ₦1.8 million and ₦4.3 million per quarter.

Mrs. Umeh also noted that the cost of the extended window would be partially offset by the reduction in lost generation. She estimated that the extended window would allow the maintenance team to complete all preventive checks and repairs in a single visit, reducing the likelihood of a breakdown occurring shortly after the maintenance visit. She noted that the plant had experienced a failure within two weeks of the last two maintenance visits, and that the extended window would allow the team to carry out a more thorough inspection of the gearboxes, including a visual inspection of the oil seals and a check of the torque settings on the mounting bolts.

**Maintenance Window Extension – Supporting Documentation**

**File Reference:** GV/CC/2025/CR-002/07
**Date of Extract:** 2025-01-10
**Prepared by:** Legal & Contracts Unit, for the attention of the Change Control Board (CCB)

**1.3 Operational Readiness and Scheduling Impact**

Engr. T. A. Bakare (Maintenance Manager) submitted a memorandum dated 2025-01-09 regarding the operational readiness for the proposed 48-hour maintenance window. He confirmed that the site maintenance crew currently operates two shifts of ten hours each, with a four-hour overlap for handover and safety briefings. Under the existing 24-hour window, this shift pattern allows for only 20 hours of effective working time, with the remaining four hours consumed by mobilisation, isolation, and re-commissioning.

Engr. Bakare noted that the extension to 48 hours would permit the crew to complete the full preventive maintenance schedule for the wind turbine gearboxes, including the inspection of high-speed and intermediate shaft bearings, without the need to defer any checks to a subsequent visit. He further noted that the extended window would also allow for the replacement of the oil filters on all three units, which was previously deferred due to time constraints. The memorandum is attached as Annex 3 to this file.

The CCB noted that the extension of the maintenance window would not affect the frequency of scheduled maintenance visits, which remains at one visit per quarter per turbine. The change would, however, require the contractor to provide an additional standby generator for the duration of the extended window, as the site’s main supply is not available during the maintenance period. Engr. Bakare confirmed that this would not constitute a change to the scope of works, but would be treated as a site facility arrangement.

**1.4 Insurance and Warranty Considerations**

Mrs. J. O. Umeh presented a legal note on the insurance implications of the extended maintenance window. She noted that the current all-risk policy covers the plant during maintenance, but the policy defines a maintenance window as a period not exceeding 24 hours. An extension to 48 hours would therefore require the insurer to be notified and the policy to be endorsed. Mrs. Umeh confirmed that the insurer had been approached informally, and that the endorsement would be issued at no additional premium, provided the extension was approved by the CCB before the end of the current policy year.

Mrs. Umeh also noted that the extended window would not affect the warranty on the gearboxes, as the warranty terms refer to the completion of the manufacturer’s recommended maintenance schedule, and not to the duration of any single maintenance visit. She confirmed that the manufacturer had been consulted, and that they had no objection to the extension, provided that the torque settings on the mounting bolts were checked and recorded in the maintenance log.

**1.5 Health, Safety, and Environment (HSE) Assessment**

The HSE Officer, Mr. F. O. Adewale, submitted a risk assessment for the extended maintenance window, dated 2025-01-08. The assessment identified two new risks associated with the extended period of work at height: the increased fatigue risk for the crew working beyond the normal 10-hour shift, and the risk of dehydration during the hot season. Mr. Adewale recommended that the crew be split into three shifts of eight hours each, with a mandatory rest period of 30 minutes between shifts. He also recommended that an additional first-aid kit be stationed at the base of each turbine.

The CCB noted that the contractor’s proposed shift pattern for the extended window was based on two shifts of 12 hours each, which would not comply with the site HSE policy. The CCB instructed the Legal & Contracts Unit to request a revised shift pattern from the contractor, and to confirm that the revised pattern would be reflected in the change order. The contractor’s response is expected by 2025-01-15.
